iFiSYMdZWDk.summary: An introduction to the Docker series that explains what Docker is and why developers, startups and large companies use it. The instructor uses a version-mismatch story between developers, testers and servers to show how Docker pins exact versions so a project runs the same everywhere.

key_points: Docker is a platform to build, share and run applications with containers
A container is described simply as a box holding everything with specific versions
Without Docker, version updates over two years break the project on a new developer's machine, the tester's machine or the server
Docker is technology independent and works with Java, PHP, Python, Node, Angular and others

62qemXJfqy0.summary: A promotional ad for a job-ready training program by Sharpener Tech. It covers projects, mock interviews and resume help, with payment due only after placement, and teaches no Docker content.

4zSTXO7z_3w.summary: Shows how to download and install Docker Desktop on Windows. It walks through the download page, the installer options and the restart needed after installation.

key_points: Search 'docker download'; the site detects your operating system
Download Docker Desktop for Windows and run the installer like a normal setup (next, accept agreement)
The installer offers Hyper-V and a desktop shortcut option; restart the system after installing
Docker works best on recent Windows (10/11); older versions like 7 may need extra steps

0NIokeWaGqM.summary: Shows how to download and install Docker Desktop on macOS. It covers picking the Apple-chip or Intel build, installing by drag and drop, and checking the version in the terminal.

key_points: Three steps: download from the official site, install, then verify from the command line
Check 'About This Mac' to choose between the Apple chip and Intel chip download
Double-click the download and drag Docker into Applications, then accept terms and use recommended settings
Run 'docker -v' in a new terminal to confirm the installed version

bSe3qawNQEY.summary: Explains the difference between Docker images and containers. An image is a read-only template of the project and a container is an isolated, runnable instance of that image.

key_points: An image is a ready-to-use, read-only template containing source code, libraries, dependencies and tools
An image cannot be updated; any change means creating a new image, and an image is never run directly
A container is a runnable instance of an image, like an object created from a class
A container is an isolated process: it uses the Node version from its image (e.g. Node 16) even if the host has Node 20

n5yO5IOtV0A.summary: Introduces Docker Hub, the online registry for searching and pulling images, and Docker Desktop, the local app installed with Docker. It also briefly introduces parent images such as Node, which you download rather than build yourself.

key_points: Docker Hub is an online tool used in the browser; Docker Desktop is installed on your machine along with Docker
Docker Hub lists images such as Node, Mongo and PHP with versions, docs and an official-image badge
Docker Desktop can also search and pull images and shows containers and volumes
The main purpose of both is to download (pull) and manage images
A React app image needs Node, so the Node image is its parent image
You build your own application image, but parent images like Node or Mongo are downloaded from Docker Hub
Images come in two types: your project's image and parent images; details are deferred to the next part
Docker Hub shows the 'docker pull node' command for an image
Pull means download; images can be pulled or run from Docker Desktop or by command

JRsD5jRSDv0.summary: Explains what a base image (also called a parent image) is and how your own project image is built on top of it. Uses Node, PHP and Python images from Docker Hub as examples of base images you pull rather than build yourself.

key_points: Base image and parent image are the same thing
Your project image depends on a base image such as Node, PHP or Python that you cannot build yourself
The base image is pulled first and your code is layered on top to make a separate image
In a Dockerfile the base image comes first, then your own additions
Building a Dockerfile produces an image
Running an image produces a container
Base images are pulled from Docker Hub with the help of Docker Desktop
Searching hub.docker.com shows official images with their pull command
Docker Hub lists the supported tags for an image so you can choose a version

hJLNs5zEasw.summary: Pulls ready-made Node and PHP images from Docker Hub, using both the Docker Desktop pull button and the docker pull command. Runs each image as a container, opens a terminal inside it and runs Node and PHP code to show the container works independently of the host.

key_points: Pulling an image is the same as downloading it
You can pull with Docker Desktop or with the docker pull command (e.g. docker pull node), and commands are the same on Mac, Windows and Linux
Running the image creates a container with an auto-generated name unless you give one
Inside the container's terminal, node and php -r commands run even though PHP is not installed on the host
Docker Desktop has a search box to find images on Docker Hub and a Pull button
Pulled images appear in Docker Desktop's Images section
The RAM, CPU and disk shown are what is assigned to Docker Desktop's virtual machine, not the whole system
The pulled Node image is the latest tag, and many other versions are listed
A container runs like its own server, independent of the Node version on your machine
Two containers can hold two different PHP versions

59vN0FcOJIA.summary: Builds a basic Node.js Express app with a root route that returns a list of users, to be dockerized in later parts. Runs it locally on port 5500 after port 5000 turns out to be in use; no Docker commands are used yet.

zeYP1rPxL3Y.summary: Writes a Dockerfile for the Node app using FROM, COPY, RUN npm install, EXPOSE and CMD, with the VS Code Docker extension for hints. Builds the image with docker build -t and checks it in Docker Desktop and with docker images, noting its 1.1 GB size comes from the Node base image.

key_points: Create a file named Dockerfile with no extension (touch Dockerfile or new file)
FROM node:latest sets the base image, COPY . . copies the project, RUN npm install installs dependencies
EXPOSE should use the same port the app listens on (5500)
CMD takes the command as an array, e.g. ["node", "index.js"]; WORKDIR sets a working folder
FROM asks for the base image, here node with the latest version
The built image is about the same size as the Node image because Node is its base
docker build -t basic-app . builds an image from the Dockerfile
-t gives the image its name and . is the build folder
The new image shows in Docker Desktop and in docker images
The image is 1.1 GB, almost all of it from the Node base image
The -t flag tags the image with a name (basic-app)
There is also a .dockerignore file, covered later

GiLj9GibpSw.summary: Runs the basic-app image as a container from Docker Desktop and shows how to assign a host port so the app is reachable in the browser. Compares a fixed port, no port (the app runs but cannot be reached from outside) and port 0, which assigns a random host port to avoid conflicts.

key_points: Clicking Run on an image in Docker Desktop creates a container from it
Optional settings let you name the container
Stopping the container makes the app unreachable and starting it again brings it back
Without a host port the container runs but cannot be reached from outside
The host port can be anything (e.g. 7000) while the app listens on 5500 inside; keeping them the same avoids confusion
Setting the host port to 0 assigns a random port (e.g. 32769) so containers never conflict
Done through Docker Desktop's optional settings, not the -p flag
The container's logs show the app's output, 'app is running on 5500'
Installing everything on a server one by one risks errors and version differences
Passing an image to the server and running it avoids those problems
The image will be taken to a server and run there, shown in a later part
Stop a container and wait a few seconds before deleting it
Containers are deleted from Docker Desktop's container list

5D6FxfrP0KA.summary: Explains the .dockerignore file, which keeps listed files and folders out of a Docker image. Shows ignoring a single file, the node_modules folder, and every file with a given extension using *.txt.

key_points: Files or folders named in .dockerignore are never added to the image
Always ignore node_modules: it is heavy and slows building, moving and running, and RUN npm install recreates it from package.json
*.txt ignores every file with the .txt extension

YUYnYsBm114.summary: Shows why and how to delete Docker images and containers, first through Docker Desktop and then from the terminal. Covers why an image in use by a container cannot be removed directly and how to force-delete images and running containers.

key_points: Images are read-only and never updated, so old images pile up and must be deleted to free server or local space
Docker Desktop has a delete option next to each image and container
An image used by any container (running, exited or stopped) cannot be deleted until that container is removed, or it is forced with -f
From the terminal, docker images lists images; a running container must be stopped or removed with -f
Docker Desktop is convenient for deleting images and containers on a local machine
On servers such as AWS or Google Cloud you will usually need the command line instead
An image is read-only and cannot be updated; a change always produces a new image
Containers are created from images, which is why an in-use image is locked
Creates extra images with docker build -t and an image name to have something to delete
Runs a couple of the new images as named containers with a port so they are in use

PKh2suGoz54.summary: Explains what a version is and why Docker images should be versioned with tags instead of given new names for each release. Demonstrates wiping everything with a prune command, building an image with a v2 tag and running that version in its own container.

key_points: A new release with UI changes, performance fixes or bug fixes is a new version, like Windows 7, 8, 10, 11
Match the image version to the project version (e.g. v10) so you know what is running on the server
Using a separate name per release gets unmanageable (5 projects x 10 versions = 50 names)
Building without a version gives the tag latest; adding :v2 to the name in docker build -t gives tag v2
docker system prune deletes all containers and images in one go after you confirm with yes
Docker Desktop may need reopening or refreshing before the deletions show
Runs the basic-app:v2 image with docker run from the terminal, giving the container its own name
The old and new versions run side by side as separate containers
The v2 container is opened on localhost on port 5500

HU1U0H184R0.summary: Explains Docker volumes as a way to keep data permanently and sync code changes into a running container without rebuilding the image. Sets up nodemon, updates the Dockerfile, and runs a container with a volume mount so edits appear live.

key_points: Data stored inside a container is temporary and is lost when the container is deleted
A volume stores data permanently and keeps it synced with the container
Without a volume, local code changes need a rebuilt image and a new container; with a volume plus nodemon they show up automatically
Mount with -v using the absolute project path (not relative) followed by :/app
Adds an npm install step to the Dockerfile so nodemon is installed in the image
Sets WORKDIR /app so the app works inside an app folder rather than the root
Rebuilds a fresh image with docker build -t after the code change; -t stands for tag
Runs the container from the command line with docker run and a container name (basic-container)
Maps the app port with -p 5500:5500, using the same port the app listens on

wdjPuDMeHS4.summary: Introduces the Docker compose file as a place to keep the long Docker commands a growing project needs. Writes a small compose.yaml with one service (build path and ports) and runs it to create the image and container.

key_points: Docker commands for building, running, ports and so on get long and hard to remember, so they go in a compose.yaml file
One compose file can cover a whole stack, such as a React frontend, Node backend and MongoDB
The file lists services; each has a build path ('.' for the current folder) and ports
Running the compose file builds the image and starts the container; a 'services not valid' error was fixed by correcting indentation

l77wncu2G1Q.summary: Explains Docker Hub as a registry of public and private images and walks through creating a repository and pushing a local image to it. Then deletes the local copy, pulls the image back from Docker Hub and runs it.

key_points: Docker Hub is a repository of images where many public images are available
Official images exist for languages and frameworks, e.g. PHP and Node
Repositories can be public or private; you sign up and log in with email and password
Create a repository on Docker Hub first; it shows the docker push command to use
Build the image locally with the repository name, then run docker login in the terminal
docker push uploads the image, using the latest tag by default; time depends on image size and internet speed
Copy the pull command from the repository's public view
docker pull with the image name downloads it; an 'authorization required' message appeared during the demo
The pulled image is then run on a port with a container name
The push uses the default latest tag, which then appears on Docker Hub

YSImafU_XMA.summary: Shows how to put an application live on a remote server using Play with Docker. Builds the image for linux/amd64, pushes it to a Docker Hub repository, then pulls and runs it on a Play with Docker instance and opens the app on port 5500.

key_points: Play with Docker is a free learning tool that keeps an app live for about four hours, not permanently
Sign in (preferably with Docker Hub) and create an instance, which gives a separate OS with Docker already installed
Pull the image using the command from the Docker Hub public view, check with docker images, then docker run -p 5500:5500
Open the app through the port link, or use 'open port' and enter 5500
Create a public repository on Docker Hub (e.g. node-demo-app)
Name the image as account-name/repository-name when building
Push it, and after refresh the latest tag shows OS/architecture linux/amd64
The usual docker build -t name . needs a platform flag to target a different OS
Play with Docker uses linux/amd64, so the build passes --platform linux/amd64
On Windows you may need the = sign in the platform flag; on Mac it worked without it
Runs with -p 5500:5500, keeping both ports the same to avoid confusion

Docker fundamentals.text: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
answer_points: An image is a read-only template with the code, libraries and tools
A container is a running instance created from an image

Docker fundamentals.text: A project works on your laptop but breaks on the tester's machine and the server. How does Docker fix this?
answer_points: The app is packaged with its dependencies at fixed versions
The same image runs the same way on every machine
Nothing has to be installed on the server one by one
A container uses its image's versions, not the host's
It works for any stack, such as Node, Java or Python

Docker fundamentals.text: What is a base image? Give an example for a Node.js app.
answer_points: The image your own image is built on top of, set with FROM
For a Node app it is the node image from Docker Hub

Building images.text: Write a Dockerfile for a Node app that listens on port 5500, and say what each line does.
answer_points: FROM node sets the base image
WORKDIR /app sets the working folder
COPY . . copies the project and RUN npm install installs dependencies
EXPOSE 5500 documents the port the app listens on
CMD ["node", "index.js"] starts the app
It is heavy and slows building and moving the image
RUN npm install recreates it inside the image from package.json

Building images.text: How do you keep version 1 and version 2 of the same image side by side?
answer_points: Tag each build with a version, such as basic-app:v2
A build without a version gets the tag latest

Building images.text: Every code change makes your image reinstall all npm packages. Why, and how do you fix it?
answer_points: Each instruction is a cached layer
COPY . . before npm install breaks the cache on any code change
Copy package.json and package-lock.json first
Run npm install in its own layer
Copy the rest of the code after

Building images.text: Your Node image is 1.1 GB. How would a multi-stage build shrink it?
answer_points: Build in a first stage that has the full toolchain
Start a second stage from a slim base image
Copy only the built output and production dependencies with COPY --from
Dev tools and sources stay out of the final image
The image gets smaller and safer

Running containers.text: Your app listens on 5500 inside the container, but localhost:5500 does not open. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
answer_points: The container's port is not published to the host
Publish it with -p hostPort:containerPort, such as -p 5500:5500
The host port can differ from the container port, such as 7000:5500
Host port 0 picks a random free port
The app must listen on the container port you publish

Running containers.text: Why can't you delete an image that a stopped container still uses?
answer_points: Containers are created from the image, so it stays locked
Remove the container first, or force it with -f

Running containers.text: You edit your code but the running container doesn't change. How do volumes help?
answer_points: Data inside a container is temporary and lost when it is deleted
A volume keeps files on the host in sync with the container
Mount it with -v using the absolute project path, such as -v /path/to/app:/app
With nodemon the app reloads on every change
No new image or container is needed for each edit

Running containers.text: A container stops right after it starts. Which commands show you why?
answer_points: docker ps -a shows the container and its exit status
docker logs shows what the app printed

Running containers.text: Your Node container must connect to a MongoDB container. How do they find each other?
answer_points: Create a user-defined network with docker network create
Attach both containers to it with --network
Containers reach each other by container name
The default bridge network has no name lookup
Only publish ports needed from outside

Shipping.text: Why use a compose file, and what goes in it for a single Node service?
answer_points: Long build and run commands are hard to remember
compose.yaml lists the services
Each service has a build path such as .
Each service lists its ports
One command builds the image and starts the container

Shipping.text: Walk through getting an image from your laptop running on a fresh server.
answer_points: Create a repository on Docker Hub
Name the image account-name/repository-name and docker push it after docker login
On the server, docker pull the image
Run it with docker run -p 5500:5500
Open the app on the published port

Shipping.text: An image built on an Apple-chip Mac won't run on a Linux server. Why, and how do you fix it?
answer_points: The image was built for a different CPU architecture
Build with --platform linux/amd64

Shipping.text: Name ways to make a production container more secure.
answer_points: Use small, official base images
Run as a non-root user
Keep secrets out of the image
Scan images for vulnerabilities
Rebuild regularly to pick up patches
